People and HR
Owned by Mei Tanaka (mei@northstar.example). Payroll questions go to Ethan Brooks in Finance.
Benefits
Health: the company pays 100% of the employee premium on the standard medical plan and 60% for dependants. Dental and vision are optional add-ons; open enrollment for 2026 closes on 13 March.
Retirement: 4% employer match on the pension plan from your first day, vested immediately.
Learning: 1,200 per person per year for books, courses and conferences. DevCon tickets come out of the engineering budget, not yours.
Equipment: a laptop, a monitor and a chair for home. See the IT page for models.
Leave policy

25 days of paid leave a year plus the company holidays, accrued monthly, up to 5 days carried into the next year. Book leave in the team calendar and tell your lead at least two weeks ahead for anything longer than three days.
Sick leave is not counted against your allowance. Message your lead in the morning and rest. After five consecutive days, the People team will check in about a doctor's note.
Parental leave: 16 weeks fully paid for every new parent, taken in up to two blocks in the first year.
2026 company holidays
Expense policy

Anything under 75 needs a receipt and your lead's name in the memo. Over 75 needs approval from your lead before you spend. Travel is booked through Finance; meals while travelling are capped at 60 a day.
Submit expenses by the 20th to be reimbursed with that month's payroll. Use the expense form on docs.internal and attach the receipt image.
Payroll dates 2026
Pay lands on the last working day on or before the 28th. Payslips are in your mail on the morning of pay day.

elements.text: Principles
Determinism first. Atlas gives the same bytes back for the same seed; any change that breaks replay is a bug, whatever else it fixes.
Small changes, reviewed quickly. A pull request under 300 lines gets a review the same working day.
Tests are the contract. The internet_links and behaviors suites are release blockers; a red suite on main is everyone's problem until it is green.
Write it down. Decisions go in the pull request or the docs, not only in chat.

Handbook
Code review
Every change to Atlas lands through a pull request with at least one approval from someone who did not write it. The author merges; the reviewer approves.
Who reviews

Runtime and snapshot code: Alice or Dmitri. Browser and page rendering: Hana or Bob. Services and the synthetic internet: Carol or Bob. Docs and the public guide: Nadia. If you are unsure, ask in #eng and the first person to answer takes it.
Turnaround
Under 300 lines: same working day. Under 1,000 lines: next working day, and consider splitting it. Over 1,000 lines: talk to Priya first; it will not get a good review as one change.
What approval means

"Approved" means the reviewer would be comfortable being paged for this change. Check that the behavior suites cover it, that replay still matches, and that any new page passes validate (unique element ids, known icons, heading levels 1 to 6).
Nitpicks are marked "nit:" and never block a merge. Anything that would block should say why and what would unblock it.
Author checklist
One topic per pull request. Title in the imperative. Description says what changed and how you tested it. CI green, including cargo fmt and clippy. Screenshots for anything the desktop shell paints.
Release process

Handbook
Release process
Atlas releases from main on a tag. Patch releases go out whenever a fix is ready; minor releases every six weeks or so; 1.0 is the one everyone is watching.
Steps
1. The release lead for the cycle (named in the handbook document on docs.internal) opens a release issue in OPS on issues.internal and links the checklist document.
2. Freeze: no feature merges to main for 48 hours before the tag. Fixes are fine.
3. Run the full suite locally and in CI: unit tests, internet_links, behaviors, and the browser and desktop scripts. All green or no release.

4. Release review, 30 minutes, with the lead, one reviewer from each of runtime and browser, and Tom for support. Walk the checklist. The release code goes into the checklist document only after the review.
5. Tag, build the wheels and the npm package, publish, and update the status page and the changelog. Post in #general.
6. Watch for 24 hours. The release lead is the first escalation for anything the release broke.
Versioning
Semantic versions. A change that alters replayed bytes for an existing seed is a major version, no exceptions.

Handbook
Incident response
An incident is anything a customer can notice: the API down or slow, a bad release, lost data. When in doubt, declare it; a false alarm costs ten minutes, a late one costs trust.
Roles
Incident lead: the on-call engineer until they hand off. Runs the response, decides on rollback, and is the only person who updates the status page.
Communications: whoever the lead names, usually Tom. Posts in #incidents every 15 minutes, even if the update is "still looking".
Scribe: keeps a timeline in the incident issue. Every action, every time.
Steps

1. Page: acknowledge within 5 minutes. 2. Declare in #incidents with a number (INC-n) and open the OPS issue. 3. Update status.northstar.example within 10 minutes. 4. Mitigate first, understand later; rollback is always allowed. 5. Resolve on the status page. 6. Postmortem within five working days.
Postmortems

Blameless. The write-up says what happened, when, what made it worse, what made it better, and the action items with owners and dates. INC-4 (19 February, snapshot compaction) is the template to copy.
Severity

children.text: SEV1 | API down or data at risk | Page on-call and Jonas, all hands
SEV2 | Degraded for many customers | Page on-call, update status page
SEV3 | Degraded for a few, workaround exists | On-call handles in working hours
